title: Maximus the Confessor
hook: punished, tradition says, for teaching that Christ had a human will; he saw the whole cosmos as a liturgy

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ladder of names: name God going down, take the names off going up. Your line was beyond every name. Who did you catch yourself sure you had figured out? Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

Night, on the Mount of Olives. Jesus has walked about a stone's throw from his friends, and he kneels down to pray. Luke gives the words: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." Not my will. So he had one. A monk named Maximus read that line and wouldn't let it go, and tradition says it cost him dearly. Today closes a week of great thinkers, with the one remembered as the Confessor.

In Maximus's day, a teaching was spreading that Christ had only one will. It was meant to keep the peace between quarreling churches. Maximus said no. If the Son of God became fully human, he became human all the way down, and a human being has a human will. In the garden we hear that will speak: remove this cup. And then we hear it freely say yes: not my will, but thine. That yes, Maximus taught, is where a human will is healed, not erased. Tradition says he was put on trial, refused to back down, and was punished with terrible cruelty and sent into exile. That's why he's called Confessor: someone who suffered for confessing the faith. Here's the larger picture he saw. Every created thing, he taught, has its own word, its own reason for being, from the one Word who made it. A stone, a sparrow, a person. And all of it is meant to be gathered back to God. Ephesians speaks of God gathering "together in one all things in Christ." Maximus saw the church at worship as a small model of that whole, and the whole world as a kind of worship. Some readers sum up his vision as a cosmic liturgy. So look back at this week. Athanasius on why the Word became flesh. The Cappadocians, three and one. Augustine's restless heart, and his picture of love. Boethius and the wheel. Dionysius and the ladder of names. And now Maximus: a human will saying yes, inside a universe at prayer.

Here's the practice: offer your will today. Settle, and breathe. Notice one thing you want badly right now, big or small. Don't pretend you don't want it. Jesus didn't pretend in the garden. Name it plainly. Then, if you pray, you can say his words from Luke: not my will, but thine, be done. If you don't pray, simply hold the wanting with an open hand instead of a fist, and breathe around it. The bell holds the time.
Maximus the Confessor. A monk who taught that Christ had a real human will that freely said yes, and who saw all creation gathered into worship.

Your line: a cosmic liturgy. Today, step outside once and watch something that isn't human, a bird, a tree, the light on a wall, and count it as part of the worship. Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor Maximus as a saint; Christians of different churches pray Jesus's words from Gethsemane, "not my will, but thine," when facing a hard choice.

he taught the opposite: Christ, fully human, had a human will, which freely said yes in the garden.

fork.setup: you're Maximus. a teaching that Christ had only one will is meant to keep the peace between churches. what do you do?
options: go along with it for the sake of peace.
say no: a fully human Christ had a human will.
fork.reveal: Maximus refused. tradition says he was tried, punished with cruelty, and exiled for it, which is why the church calls him Confessor.

original.note: Greek: word, reason. Maximus taught that each created thing has its own logos from the one Logos, the Word.

trapdoor: what you thought: if Jesus is God, he couldn't have wanted anything different.
what it means: Maximus taught Christ had a real human will, which said remove this cup, then freely said not my will, but thine.
what a scholar hears: two wills in one person, and a cosmos where every thing's own logos is gathered back to the Logos.

notes: Week close (days 1240–1246): the look-back lists each day's theme from the index; days 1240 and 1241 were not yet written when this was drafted, so confirm the one-line summaries match those scripts.

Index hook says 'tortured'; the script says 'tradition says he was put on trial ... punished with terrible cruelty and sent into exile' (the traditional accounts include cutting out his tongue and cutting off his right hand). No date given. Confirm.

The one-will teaching (monothelitism) is described as 'meant to keep the peace between quarreling churches'; confirm this is fair. Maximus's reading of Gethsemane (the human will healed by freely agreeing) is paraphrased; check against the Disputation with Pyrrhus and Opuscula.
'Some readers sum up his vision as a cosmic liturgy' alludes to Hans Urs von Balthasar's book title without naming it; confirm.
Logoi of creatures (Ambigua 7) and church as image of cosmos (Mystagogy) are paraphrased; check.

Editor pass: the hook cited Luke but used Matthew's detail (face to the ground) and John's garden; it now follows Luke 22:39–41 (Mount of Olives, a stone's cast, kneeled down). 'The one the church calls the Confessor' softened to 'the one remembered as the Confessor'. The garden in the teach and practice is kept as the familiar name for the scene.
howItsDone: Maximus is commemorated as a saint by Orthodox and Catholic Christians; confirm. Original λόγος: confirm accent/pronunciation.

Audit (2026-10-02): 'only one will, a divine one' trimmed to 'only one will'; monothelete formulas spoke of one will without always calling it simply divine. Week look-back checked against days 1240 and 1241: matches.
